$description: The design system token layer: settings (the knobs), primitives (the computed scales and the colour ramps) and the semantic roles. Dark-theme values ride on the token they belong to, under $extensions.

org.css-design-system.source: styles/*.css — edit the CSS, never this file
org.css-design-system.spec: Design Tokens Community Group format, colors and dimensions as typed objects

5.$description: 20. Added 2026-08-26 on the owner's call, and the reason is a real gap: the ladder doubled after 4 and jumped 16 → 24, so a distance a screen genuinely wanted between those two could only be reached by stacking two tokens — and a sum is not a decision. The page audit reads the scale rather than a copy of it, so it accepted this step the moment it existed.

grid-unit.$description: Space — grid-unit is the SINGLE base unit (4pt grid). All --space-* in primitives.css are integer multiples of it. Fixed: it's a decision, not a live knob — to retune density, change it here in source.

2xs.$description: sub-grid hairline (badge pad, switch thumb gap, dividers)

section.$description: Fluid spacing for section gaps (grows with viewport width)

md.$description: 17px — large body / subheads (fills the base→lg gap)

light.$description: Weights — all four are real faces, not synthesised: both brand families are VARIABLE fonts, so one file per script covers the whole range (see brand/system/manifest.json). A brand shipping static files must supply one per weight, or the browser fakes the missing ones.

default.$description: base (md) radius — keep a multiple of the grid

rect.$description: base (md) radius — keep a multiple of the grid

sm.$description: Radius — scale steps by the grid unit, so every tier stays on-grid. (--radius is the md tier; sm is one grid step down, lg/xl steps up.)

fast.$description: Motion. Durations AND the curve, because a duration without a curve is half a decision: everything that had no `transition-timing-function` fell back to CSS `ease`, which starts fast and ends slow — the shape a thing makes when it is thrown, not when it answers. One curve for the system. --ease-out is THE curve: fast off the mark, settling into the end state. --ease-in-out is for something that leaves and comes back (a drawer, a carousel slide), where both ends need to be soft. The rule the card was breaking (owner, 23.08: the animation on the cards is jerky, it should be smooth and crisp): ONE gesture moves at ONE speed. The hover used to run a 120ms shadow, a 200ms scrim and a 320ms zoom at once, so the parts of a single card arrived one after another.

width.$description: Focus ring — single source for the universal focus-visible outline.

shadow-popover.$description: Elevation — shadows shared by cards/popovers (shadow-sm/md/lg in primitives).

shadow-card-hover.$description: Soft, and actually visible. It was 0 0 24px at 6% black — a glow so faint that the only feedback a card gave under the pointer was the cursor. A lift has a direction: a small downward offset reads as the card coming up off the page, which is what the gesture means.

muted-foreground.$description: neutral-700, not -600: secondary text also sits on --muted surfaces (the app background, table heads, side panels), where -600 reached only 4.15:1 and missed AA. -700 is 5.57:1 there and 6.04:1 on white, and still reads as clearly secondary against --foreground (neutral-900, 15.8:1).

primary-active.$description: Pressed. Hover moves one stop, the press moves one more — the third step the system did not have.

link.$description: LINKS. There was no such token and no Link component, so every link in the system had picked its own colour by hand: the link-button brand, EntityLink near-black, the breadcrumb grey, a card title inheriting. Four answers to one question, side by side on the same screen. One decision now: --link text that goes somewhere, inside reading text --link-quiet the same thing in chrome, where position already says it Deliberately NOT :visited: these are application links, and a workspace whose nav recolours itself as you use it reads as broken rather than as helpful. A content site should add it here and nowhere else.

primary-accent.$description: Primary used as TEXT / icon / border ON a page or card surface (not a fill). Same as --primary in light; the dark theme lightens it so brand-blue accents stay legible on the dark surface (brand-400 there sits at ~1.7:1 — it blends). Fills (buttons, the blue action band, primary badges) keep --primary.

primary-soft.$description: Soft brand surface — tinted bg + saturated text (selected chips, soft badges, info toast).

ai.$description: AI accent — anything the assistant generated or is about to. Violet on purpose, so it never collides with the product's own brand colour after a re-skin.

chart-1.$description: ════ CHARTS ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════ The series slots a chart paints with, in fixed order: series 1 is always --chart-1, whatever else is on screen, so a filter that drops a series never repaints the ones that stay. Status colours (--success, --warning, --destructive) are NOT in this list on purpose: a chart that means "how much of it is bad" tones by meaning, and a chart that means "these are three different things" tones by slot. Mixing them makes one series look like a warning.

chart-grid.$description: The furniture: a grid line is the quietest thing on the plot, an axis label is ordinary secondary text, and the track is what an unfilled bar sits in.

chart-success.$description: Status, as DATA rather than as a chip. A donut painted in --success / --warning / --destructive came out olive, mustard and brick (owner, 23.08: this looks bad): those steps are chosen to carry white TEXT on a small badge, and a 40px arc of the same colour is a different job. These are the same three meanings, one step fresher, and they are only ever used for a filled area that carries its own label. They are deliberately NOT run through the categorical adjacency gate: a status palette separates by meaning and ships with a named legend, which is the documented mitigation.

secondary.$description: plain light grey on white surfaces; page-level contexts override to white

accent-soft.$description: neutral-200, not -100: at -100 this token WAS --muted, so a ghost button or a menu row hovering on the page surface painted itself the exact colour of the page — 1.00:1, a hover that does not happen. The step has to differ from every surface it can land on, not merely be quiet.

accent-strong.$description: One stop past --accent: the hover step for a control that already carries a fill (a pill, a filled icon button), so hovering moves it FURTHER from the surface behind it rather than back towards it.

accent-active.$description: One past --accent-strong: the pressed step for a control on a card, where hover has already spent --accent-strong.

surface-contrast.$description: WHAT A QUIET CONTROL FILLS ITSELF WITH SO IT DOES NOT DISSOLVE INTO ITS SURFACE: on grey go white, on white go grey. This is the page's answer. Every surface that is NOT the page has to give its own, and that is the part which used to be missing: only `.card` did, so a quiet button on any other white area took this answer and stood white on white. `.content-surface` in the showcase is exactly that — a white area the code calls "not a card" — and its Start Editing button had no fill at all (owner, 2026-08-23). The rule was right; it was only bound in one file. A surface answering is now checked rather than remembered: the showcase's `npm run controls` walks every screen and measures every filled control against the colour actually painted behind it.

surface-contrast-active.$description: The third step: what the same control fills itself with WHILE PRESSED. The system had hover and then nothing — no `:active` rule existed anywhere in 106 components, so a click gave no answer until the work finished and a slow action read as a dead button. One more stop in the same direction.

popover-hover.$description: Hover/active fill for a row inside a POPOVER surface, which is a different surface from the page. In dark, --accent-soft and --popover are both neutral-820: every menu highlight was painting itself the exact colour of the menu (1.00:1), so hover and the keyboard position were invisible. A popover states its own step.

surface-hover.$description: Row/area hover on a card surface: one whisper lighter than the page tint, so a hovered table row reads without ever matching --muted (a hover that equals the page colour looks like a hole, not a highlight).

nav-active.$description: Left as it was: ChatHistory is its consumer and paints hover/active with it. The sidebars keep their own --accent background — the two surfaces differ on purpose, and a contrast fix for dark mode is no reason to restyle either.

success.$description: Status roles — components use these, never the success/warning/danger primitive stops. Each tone: solid fill + on-fill text, a soft tint + its text, and an emphasis tone for icons/accents. (danger == --destructive.)

success-emphasis.$description: Ink, not fill: success-700 is 3.71:1 on white. success-800 is 5.25:1 and is already what the solid fill uses, so the two read as the same green.

warning-soft-foreground.$description: Dark ink on the yellow tint: warning-900 is a mid orange and only reached 2.3:1 on warning-100. Matches --warning-foreground on the solid fill.

warning-emphasis.$description: The INK, not the fill. warning-700 is the bright yellow the solid badge is filled with, and as text on white it sits at 1.54:1 — the `plain` warning badge was effectively invisible. warning-950 is the dark amber the palette already carried for exactly this, at 13.88:1. Found by axe in a real browser; the token-level contrast check never tested this pair.

destructive-emphasis.$description: Ink, not fill: danger-500 is 3.29:1 on white. danger-800 is 4.98:1, the same stop --destructive already uses.

success-border.$description: Edge of a soft-tinted surface. A tint alone only reads on a surface it does not match: an info notice on --muted, or a success notice on a pale card, dissolved into the page. The border is what makes the shape survive any background, so every tinted status surface carries one. Chosen per ramp by eye, not by a fixed stop offset: the yellow ramp stays pale until 700, so two stops up from the tint would be invisible there.

control-edge.$description: THE EDGE A CONTROL DRAWS SO ITS SHAPE SURVIVES ANY SURFACE. --surface-contrast answers "what do I fill myself with"; this answers "and where do I end". They are two different questions, and the arithmetic says so: no fill can be quiet enough to read as secondary AND separated enough to clear 3:1 — solved numerically over the whole ramp, there is no such colour. So the fill stays quiet and the edge carries the boundary.

switch-track-off.$description: Switch track when off — semantic so dark theme can override cleanly.

avatar.$description: Avatar fallback (no image) — distinctive surface with foreground contrast.

media-ratio.$description: The picture keeps its SHAPE, not its height. A fixed 9rem made the same card's media a 2.6:1 letterbox in a grid column and a 5.2:1 strip across a feature row, so the same component looked like two different ones on one screen (owner, 22.08: the cards do not look designed).

title-size.$description: every <CardTitle> / section head. md read as body text beside 13px meta (owner, 2026-08-21); lg makes the rank visible at card-grid glance distance.

radius.$description: Popover surfaces (dropdown / select / menu) — concentric radii: the surface rounds like a small card; rows inside round one step less.

stroke.$description: line thickness for all icons (= Lucide default; 1.5 read too thin)

max-width.$description: cap for header + main content (was 80rem; one tier up)

The whole shell: nav column + capped content. Past this the composition stops growing and centres on the screen instead, so a 2560px monitor gets equal margins on both sides rather than a nav pinned to the left edge and a content column that reads 130px right of centre. 112rem = the 96rem cap plus the 16.25rem nav, rounded to the scale.

50.$description: @brand:colors — regenerated by `npm run rebrand` from brand/<active>/manifest.json

550.$description: THE EDGE STOP. The one neutral that clears 3:1 against every surface this system paints, in both themes: white 3.48, page 3.20, accent 3.04, popover 3.76, card 4.20, dark page 4.54. Added because the top of this ramp is compressed — white to neutral-300 is 1.30:1 — so no existing stop could carry the boundary of a control (WCAG 1.4.11 wants 3:1). Everything that says "this is a control, and it ends here" resolves to this: --input, --switch-track-off, --control-edge.

820.$description: dark-theme subtle border (between card and accent)

850.$description: dark-theme card elevation step (subtle above bg)

900.$description: dark-theme card elevation step (subtle above bg)

50.$description: Success (Lime green, pivots around #84BD00 at the 500 stop; 800 stays the primary text/surface stop, dark enough for white-on-green).

950.$description: Dark-theme tinted SURFACE. The yellow ramp never gets dark (900 is a saturated orange), so dark mode had no legible soft-warning background — this stop is that surface. Not part of the light ramp.
Dark-theme tinted SURFACE — same reason as --warning-950: the coral ramp stays light enough that danger-900 cannot host readable text in dark mode.

0.$description: Scrim stops: the ink-alpha ramp under text that sits over imagery. Alpha on a near-black, never on pure black — pure black scrims go muddy.

50.$description: Violet — the AI accent. Deliberately outside the brand ramp: "generated by the assistant" has to read as a different KIND of thing from the product's own colour, in every brand this system is re-skinned into.

1.$description: Series 1 IS the brand, and now says so rather than repeating its hex. The comment always claimed the relationship; the code did not, so a rebrand moved the brand and left chart series 1 on the old indigo (audit, 2026-08-26). Same for its dark step.

6-dark.$description: This green reads on both surfaces, so its dark step is the light one — stated, not coincidentally retyped.

sticky.$description: Z-index — sticky lowest, then modals, then dropdowns (so Selects inside a Modal render above it), then toasts, then tooltips on top.
